metadata.description: Single-plugin marketplace exposing the cc-enslaver discipline plugin.

plugins.name: cc-enslaver
plugins.description: Rules your coding agent physically cannot ignore. A Claude Code plugin (and LLM-agnostic rule pack) that stops reactive patching, guessed citations, surface-level fixes and premature "done" claims by intercepting the agent's own tool calls rather than asking it nicely. PreToolUse denies an edit before it lands — editing a file you never opened this session, a suppression marker with no adjacent why-comment, a hardcoded secret or user-home path, the fourth small patch to one file, a dangerous shell flag. A nine-layer Stop gate then refuses to let a completion claim end the turn without evidence, a convergence self-quiz, a fidelity check against the user's ORIGINAL request, and a one-line TL;DR. Twelve rules, eight backed by a hook; "Imperial Edict" regexes you define per project; a repo-wide sync gate; three CI drift gates that derive every documented number from the code so the documentation cannot rot. Zero dependencies, stdlib only, Linux + Windows CI, and every guard fails OPEN — a bug in the discipline can never brick your agent. v0.31.0 makes the rule-12 sync gate INSPECTABLE. Its co-update groups have been enforceable since v0.23 and authorable only by hand-writing TOML, with no way to see what the loader made of it — and that loader is failing-open by design, so a dropped group or a glob matching no file does not raise; it simply stops guarding, printing one stderr line nobody reads. An unenforced gate you still trust is worse than no gate, because you have stopped looking at it. The new `/cc-enslaver:sync-gate` command (init / list / check / add / remove / path) closes the hole: `check` reports every group the loader kept, every group it DROPPED and why, and every glob matching no file in the repo, exiting 1 so it can run in CI. Deliberately NOT auto-created: no hook writes into the user's project directory — an invariant that has held for every release — and an auto-created empty template would be functionally identical to no file at all (zero groups means Stop layer (i) stays inert), bought at the price of an unrequested file in everyone's git status. Writes are verified twice, not once: not merely "does this parse" but "does the loader still keep every group", because a `require = []` entry is perfectly valid TOML that sync_gate.load() silently discards — a parse-only check would let the CLI report success over a group that guards nothing. On failure the previous file is restored byte-for-byte. One defect found during this feature's own first smoke test is reported here rather than quietly fixed: the CLI chose its write target with config_path(), the resolver built for READING, which tries several candidate roots and takes the first that already holds a file — so a run targeting a project with no config yet fell through to the process cwd and appended two groups to this plugin's own config. The root cause is that "where do I read from" and "where do I write to" are different questions, and a read-resolver's fallback chain is precisely what makes it the wrong answer to the second. Fixed at the mechanism (default_project_path, deterministic; load_file, no fallback), swept across both call sites, and the read resolver's fallback is now pinned by its own test so a later "make them both deterministic" cannot silently break the hook path. Also, lib/tomlio.py now owns the TOML writer alongside the reader, so the edict CLI and the sync-gate CLI share one encoder rather than letting the second copy miss the next fix. 565 → 590 tests. Prior — v0.30.0 was a structural audit of the plugin itself, on one theme: a thing that is written down is not a thing that is enforced. Seven unreachable production symbols were deleted rather than annotated, among them a retired rationale checker left standing beside the live one — where the next reader has no way to tell which of the two the guard actually consults — and an `_escape_triple_quoted` marked "kept only so an external caller does not break" that no caller could reach. Three duplicated judgements were collapsed to one definition each: markdown fence parsing existed in three copies, each carrying its own transcription of the same v0.25 CommonMark fix, and the project-root predicate existed twice with the second annotated "same project-root heuristic as lib/edicts.py" — a comment that names an invariant without holding it, so widening one copy silently leaves the other behind (new shared module: lib/projroot.py). And the Stop status table stopped making a claim of its own kind: layers are DISPLAYED (a) through (i) but EVALUATED with (b) first, because a hedge invalidates a done-claim however much evidence sits beside it — yet the table derived both "Pass" and "pending" from the display index, so every hedge block printed "(a) PASS", asserting that convergence evidence had been found on a turn where `_has_evidence` was never called. A gate built to catch unfounded claims does not get to make one; fixed, with twin tests in both directions. The file tree was reclassified rather than rearranged: test files are named for what they cover and indexed file-by-file in tests/README.md, hooks/scripts/ labels its three roles inline, and docs/ gained an index. The four non-hook scripts deliberately did NOT move into a tools/ directory — gc_state.py is imported by inject_context.py for auto-GC and register_read.py's real logic lives inside bash_guard.py, so neither is a standalone CLI and the move would trade a tidier directory name for a real cross-tree sys.path splice. CLAUDE.md shrank from 87 KB to 39 KB: its "current version" section had grown into a verbatim second copy of the changelog, re-read into context on every single session and free to drift from the original. 564 → 565 tests, all green on Linux and Windows. Full release history lives in CHANGELOG.md, which is now its only copy.
